title: Quiz: Floating Point - Fundamentals
prompt: Work through the single and double precision register views, the directives that place floating-point values in memory, the operand rules the arithmetic instructions follow, and the gdb format that reads a register as a number.

questions.question: A double precision value sits in a d register. How many bits wide is that register?
questions.explanation: A d register is the low-order 64 bits of one of the 128-bit vector registers, and holds one double precision value. An s register is the low-order 32 bits of the same register and holds a single precision value.
questions.hint: The d stands for double, which is twice the width of a 32-bit single precision float.

questions.question: Which directive places a double precision constant in .data?
questions.explanation: .double assembles its value as an 8-byte IEEE 754 double, the size a d register loads. .float assembles a 4-byte single for an s register, while .dword and .word place 8-byte and 4-byte integers.
questions.hint: Match the directive to the register: 8 bytes of floating-point data for a d register.

questions.question: An assembly subroutine returns a double precision result to a C caller. Which register holds the return value?
questions.explanation: A double precision result comes back in d0, and a single precision result in s0. Integer and pointer results come back in x0, so a caller reading x0 after a floating-point function reads the wrong register.
questions.hint: It is the lowest-numbered register of the size that matches the result.

questions.question: How do the basic floating-point arithmetic instructions such as fadd and fmul differ from their integer counterparts in the operands they accept?
options: They take register operands only and accept no immediate value.
They require a memory address as the third operand.
They set the condition flags without needing an s suffix.
questions.explanation: fadd, fsub, fmul and fdiv take register operands only, so a constant has to be in an s or d register before the arithmetic runs. They also leave the condition flags alone; fcmp is what sets them.
questions.hint: Load your floating-point constants into registers before doing arithmetic with them.

questions.question: In gdb, which print format shows a register value as a floating-point number?
questions.explanation: The f format letter tells print to show a value as floating point, so p/f is the format that reads a value as a number instead of a bit pattern. p/d prints decimal and p/x prints hex, and x/ examines memory at an address instead of printing a value.
questions.hint: The format letter is the first letter of float, and p prints a value while x examines memory.
